# HISTORY
### *CRITICAL*
## OF ECLECTICISM.

->VOLUME ONE.<-

<vocab>history, critical, eclecticism, volume one</vocab>

<note>A "critical history" in the 18th century was not merely a list of dates, but an analytical evaluation of the truth and logic behind historical ideas.</note>

<note>Eclecticism refers to a philosophical method that does not adhere to a single school of thought, but instead selects and combines the most sound doctrines from various traditions, such as those of Plato, Aristotle, or the Stoics.</note>

<summary>This title page marks the beginning of Guillaume de Maleville's scholarly examination of Eclecticism, presenting it as a "critical history" in the Enlightenment tradition. It formally introduces the first volume of a work intended to synthesize diverse philosophical viewpoints into a coherent system.</summary>

# PREFACE.

*The importance of the love of truth. Why, along with the* Encyclopedist <note>Likely referring to Denis Diderot, the primary editor of the *Encyclopédie* and author of the article on "Eclecticism"</note>, *Author of the article on* Eclecticism <note>A school of philosophy that does not hold to a single paradigm but draws upon multiple theories to gain complementary insights into a subject</note>, *we also attack* Mr. Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a German historian whose "Critical History of Philosophy" was a primary source for the *Encyclopédie*</note> *in several parts of this* Work. *How little the* Encyclopedist *has respected the truth. Proof of this accusation.*

<header>PREFACE.</header>

—were always the faithful disciples of truth, and its sincere friends. A love for truth makes for a man of integrity <note>The original French *honnête homme* refers to the 17th and 18th-century social and moral ideal of a person of integrity, refined culture, and virtue.</note> and a man of religion: a fortunate resource, which sets us on the path of happiness, or brings us back to it sooner or later, when the misfortune of birth <note>Refers to being born into a culture or family that holds erroneous beliefs.</note> or the power of deception has cast us into error.

The Creator has formed our minds for the true, and we could have no attraction to what is false. Thus, it is not strictly a hatred for truth, but rather an indifference toward it, that can be blamed on those without virtue. They cling to error only for the sake of interests they lack the strength to sacrifice for this love of truth. A sound philosophy nevertheless makes us feel that this disposition, so common among me— <note>The original French text "hom-" is a truncation of "hommes" (men), cut off by the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page argues that humans are naturally inclined toward truth by the Creator, and that "error" is usually the result of social conditioning or selfish interests rather than a genuine hatred of truth. It defines the love of truth as the essential characteristic of both a virtuous man and a religious man.</summary>

<keywords>truth, virtue, integrity, religion, Creator, philosophy, human nature, error</keywords>

<page-num>vij</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

—men, is very condemnable. But it appears much more fatal and more criminal in the eyes of Religion. For it is only by the light of truth that God wishes to lead rational creatures to their perfection, which is inseparable from their happiness. God excuses errors that are invincible <note>Theological term "invincible error" refers to a mistake made by someone who, despite their best efforts, could not have known the truth.</note>. But even invincible errors are not the means He has established to make us reach our destination.

As indifference toward truth is a lack of respect and love for the Sovereign Truth, and since this indifference leads to all kinds of disorder, leading as it does to pyrrhonism <note>A school of extreme skepticism that suggests one should suspend judgment on all matters because certainty is impossible.</note> and irreligion; the first step to return to order is a sincere return to the love of truth. It is she <note>The author personifies Truth, which is a feminine noun in the original French.</note> who prescribes all our du— <note>The sentence is truncated at "de-" (part of "devoirs" or duties) and continues on the following page.</note>

Thus, what more fertile cause of evil is there than to accustom oneself, and to accustom others, to obscure the truth, and to shroud it in clouds that prevent us from discerning it from that which bears only some deceptive resemblance to it!

Truth, often bothersome and inconvenient, knows neither compromise nor indulgence for our inclinations, or for our weaknesses. It is an iron rule that cannot be bent; and such is the strength of its dominion that one would not dare to declare oneself its enemy. When one wages war against it, it is under its own banners, and while claiming to be faithful to it. Another observation. Reliable writers do not say that *Constantine*, in wanting to build a new city, gave thought to *Chalcedon* <note>An ancient maritime town in Bithynia, Asia Minor, located almost directly opposite Byzantium.</note>, whose situation was not comparable to that of *Constantinople*. Those who built *Chalcedon* in *Asia*, instead of having placed it in *Europe* and in the place where *Byzantium* was on the other side of the *Bosphorus*, were, it was said (1), "blind men." <note>This refers to a famous anecdote from Herodotus: the founders of Chalcedon were called "blind" because they chose their site seventeen years before Byzantium was founded, overlooking the obviously superior harbor across the strait.</note> It was in the *Troad* <note>The region in northwest Asia Minor surrounding the ancient city of Troy.</note>, and near *Ilium* <note>The Latin name for Troy.</note>, that *Constantine* wanted to build his new city. In the time (2) of *Sozomen* <note>original: "Sozomene." Salaminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note> one could see the remains of this undertaking, which *Constantine* abandoned by order of Heaven, according to what this historian claims.

When it comes to miraculous events, nothing can compensate for the lack of reliable witnesses.

The events that testify to the Divinity of Christianity are odious to the Encyclopedist. If he cannot refute them with solid reasons, he turns them into ridicule; he evades their consequences; he insinuates that the Pagans also had miracles to establish the cult of their Idols; he would like to make people believe that the miracles of Paganism had hardly less authenticity than our own. This way of proceeding, however, did not yet have a constant form before <term>Potamon</term> <note>Potamon of Alexandria was a philosopher who lived during the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD; he is traditionally credited with creating the Eclectic sect to bridge the gaps between existing philosophies.</note> founded his school of Eclecticism in Alexandria, six or seven centuries after the love of wisdom <note>A literal translation of the Greek word *philosophia* (philosophy).</note> had followers separated, by profession, from the rest of men, and uniquely occupied with the search for truth. For, as (1) Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was a Roman statesman and philosopher who often leaned toward the Academic Skeptic school, which valued weighing different arguments.</note> claimed regarding the philosophers of his time, people found themselves committed to the sentiments of a sect before they were even capable of judging them. A friend would lead them to a school; they would hear the discourse of a professor, and they would become attached to him. Certain specific circumstances led them to one party rather than another, and they would fix themselves there as if to a rock. They decided by chance which master deserved preference based on the vague presumption that he was a wise man, to whose discernment

It seems that finally, people became ashamed of such an unreasonable way of acting. It was understood that one was a philosopher only insofar as one saw and examined things for oneself—in a word, only insofar as one was an *Eclectic*. <note>The term "Eclectic" comes from the Greek *eklektikos*, meaning "selective." It describes a philosopher who does not follow one single system but picks the best elements from various schools of thought.</note> But through a gross contradiction, people entered the school of the *Eclectics* only to, in a way, renounce Eclecticism. For this method of philosophy, which had been reached so late and after having tested so many errors, was no sooner discovered than it was abandoned in practice. *Eclecticism* consists of not subjecting oneself to any master, and of choosing, after a serious examination, what appears true in each sect. But this fine plan was nothing but pure speculation, and it vanished almost as soon as it had been formed. The students of the *Eclectic* school attached themselves to the opinions of their professors, just as people did in the schools of the <term>Stoics</term> <note>Followers of Zeno of Citium who taught that virtue is the only good and that we should remain indifferent to external events.</note>, the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus who sought peace and freedom from fear through the pursuit of modest pleasures and knowledge.</note>, the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named from the Greek word for "walking," as Aristotle often walked while teaching.</note>, and so on. The master, once again, thought for those he instructed, and decided which opinions were to be adopted or rejected,

### Concerning Eclecticism:

The disciples of the Eclectic philosophers were not truly Eclectics at all. The opinions of the masters prevailed, formed a body of doctrine, and established a succession just like in the other sects. Nevertheless, those who studied in the schools of these philosophers and who claimed to follow their method are called Eclectics. They were also called Alexandrian philosophers because it was in Alexandria that Potamon and Ammonius Saccas <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD) was a self-taught philosopher from Alexandria often credited as one of the founders of Neoplatonism.</note> taught. But they were designated even more frequently by the name of **Neo-Platonists**; because, without attaching themselves solely to <term>Plato</term> <note>The famous Athenian philosopher and student of Socrates whose ideas on forms and the soul deeply influenced Western thought.</note>, they had a greater preference for his views than for those of other philosophers.

The beginnings of this philosophy are very obscure. Potamon, who was the first to follow it, taught it in Alexandria: but antiquity has preserved almost nothing of Potamon for us. We are not even certain of the time in which he lived. It is, however, more likely that it was toward the end of the second century. (1) We have only a single text from <term>Suidas</term> <note>original: "Suidas." Referring to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia that serves as a vital source for ancient history and literature.</note>...

One cannot say precisely at what time Diogenes Laertius wrote his history of the philosophers. It is more likely that it was after the start of the third century, as conjectured by Mr. <term>Tillemont</term> <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French historian renowned for his meticulous scholarship on the Roman Empire and the early Church.</note>, *third volume* of the Emperors, *page 36, column 1, of the folio edition,* and Mr. <term>Brucker</term> <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), author of the influential *Critical History of Philosophy*.</note> *volume II, page 200 and following, and page 624.* Some have imagined that the *a little while ago* <note>original Latin: "Paulò ante," Greek: "Pro oligou"</note> of Diogenes Laertius should be understood in relation to the antiquity of the other philosophical sects, which had originated several centuries before this historian. However, if Eclecticism had begun in the time of Augustus, more than two hundred years earlier, Diogenes Laertius could not have said that this sect was born recently, or that it had only just come into being.

# Critical History

Eclectic philosophy <term>Eclectic</term> <note>From the Greek *eklegein*, meaning "to select." This school of thought did not follow one single set of rules but chose the best doctrines from various systems.</note>, before the end of the second century. This is also the opinion of Mr. Brucker <term>Brucker</term> <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a German historian whose work *Historia Critica Philosophiae* was a standard reference during the Enlightenment.</note> and the Encyclopedist <term>Encyclopedist</term> <note>A contributor to the *Encyclopédie*, the massive 18th-century French compendium of knowledge edited by Diderot and d’Alembert.</note>. It is a mistake, but a mistake so gross that one must blame it on the printer or the copyist; it is, I say, a mistake to say that *Potamon* (1) <term>Potamon</term> <note>A philosopher of Alexandria who sought to reconcile different philosophical systems.</note> was born under *Alexander Severus* <term>Alexander Severus</term> <note>Roman Emperor who reigned from 222 to 235 AD.</note>. This prince, after a reign of thirteen years, was killed in the year two hundred and thirty-five of Jesus Christ. *Ammonius Saccas* <term>Ammonius Saccas</term> <note>A teacher in Alexandria (c. 175–242 AD) often regarded as one of the founders of Neoplatonism; his students included Plotinus and Origen.</note> was teaching in Alexandria at that time.

The Encyclopedist, following in this the footsteps of Messrs. Brucker and *Mosheim* <term>Mosheim</term> <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), an influential Lutheran church historian.</note>, attributes to Ammonius the project of combating Christianity <note>original: *Chriſtianiſme*</note> through a system formed of what he found best in the philosophers and in Christianity itself. This is a favorite idea of these writers, to which they have given all possible plausibility, and upon which they have subsequently built a kind of history of the beginnings of Neoplatonism <note>original: *nouveau Platoniſme*</note>. Thus, before going any further, it is necessary to examine its foundation; it is necessary, I say, to examine whether Ammonius was an apostate from Christianity.

In whom should we place our trust: the Platonic philosopher <note>Referring to Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a critic of Christianity who claimed the philosopher Ammonius abandoned Christianity for paganism.</note> or the Ecclesiastical Historian <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), who maintained that Ammonius remained a Christian throughout his life.</note>? Let us decide by means of a very simple reflection. It would have been impossible for the people of Alexandria to have forgotten what the religion of Ammonius <term>Ammonius</term> <note>Ammonius Saccas (3rd century AD), the teacher of both Plotinus and Origen, and a foundational figure in the development of Neoplatonism.</note> had been. He was one of the most celebrated philosophers. He had introduced a new method of philosophizing there, which had only been sketched out before him, and which he had greatly perfected. Ammonius had taught there for a very long time to a great gathering of disciples. If he were a Christian, he would have sown many things favorable to the dogmas of Christianity throughout his lessons. Thus, the Christians must have preserved a very cherished memory of him. What Eusebius says about it leads to this very idea.

A man of mature age, who for ten or fifteen years attached himself to a Professor (for such was the custom at that time), could not leave him without being thoroughly instructed in what he taught, his method, and everything regarding his personal history. # Critical History

[Am]monius <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD) was a philosopher from Alexandria often credited as one of the founders of Neoplatonism. He was famously the teacher of Plotinus.</note> could not fail to shake off a yoke that imposes the necessity of believing all the dogmas of Christianity, without exception. If one has any doubt on this matter, let us be assured that it will not last long.

> "Ammonius the Eclectic," says the Encyclopedist <note>A reference to the authors of the *Encyclopédie* (1751–1772); the critique likely targets the "Électisme" article, largely based on the work of Johann Jakob Brucker.</note>, "did not write at all; this is what distinguishes him from the Ammonius mentioned by Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian of the early Christian Church who argued that Ammonius remained a Christian for his entire life.</note>. He imposed upon his disciples a profound silence regarding the nature and object of his lessons. He feared that the disputes which would inevitably arise between his disciples and other philosophers would increase the contempt for philosophy and the scandal <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to a "stumbling block" or cause for spiritual offense to those of weak faith.</note> of small minds. This is very consistent with what we read about him in Hierocles <note>Hierocles of Alexandria was a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>."

The only truth here is that Ammonius wrote no works on philosophy. But as for what his motives were in this, the Encyclopedist is merely guessing. The ancients do not say, and Hierocles says it no more than the others. We will shortly provide a summary of his text. Thus, what are we to judge of the speech to his disciples that the Encyclopedist attributes to Ammonius?

Now, no one was as fit to give them this knowledge as **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD), a mysterious and influential teacher in Alexandria, often credited as a founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, whether because of his learning or his method of philosophizing.

He aimed, as much as possible, to reconcile the **Sects** <note>In this context, "Sects" refers to the various competing schools of ancient philosophy, such as Platonism, Aristotelianism, Stoicism, and Epicureanism.</note> with one another, and to choose from them whatever he found most reasonable, in order to form a body of doctrine preferable to the systems of any single Sect. The manner in which (1) **Origen** instructed his disciples was no different. For he first excluded everything that could inspire impiety by attacking the **Divinity** and **Providence** <note>Providence refers to the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note>. Then he had them read all other books, and he helped his pupils discern the good from the bad, so they could adopt the former and reject the latter. Nothing could be more in line with the method of Ammonius, if he were a Christian. But there is no reason to assert that such was his method, assuming he were an enemy of Christianity.

### ARTICLE II.

## *A Brief History of Eclecticism, or of Neoplatonism, until its extinction in the time of Justinian.*

Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD), the teacher of both the Christian Origen and the philosopher Plotinus.</note> died a Christian. We are justified in asserting this; consequently, he did not teach his disciples the system that dominated the schools of the **Neoplatonists** <note>The "New Platonists," a school of thought that sought to synthesize Greek philosophy into a mystical framework.</note>, a system which turned the most famous followers of this philosophical **Sect** into **Fanatics**. **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founding figure of Neoplatonism, whose works were collected in the *Enneads*.</note> was their master, at least regarding the core of the system. He aspired to the vision of God and to **extasies** <note>Mystical states of union with the divine.</note>. He prided himself on having attained them. He believed himself superior to the **spirits of the lower order** <note>original: "Génies du bas ordre." In Neoplatonic cosmology, these are intermediary beings (daemons) that exist between humans and the divine.</note>. He passed this same "illness" on to his disciple **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), who edited Plotinus’s writings and was a sharp critic of early Christianity.</note>, who wrote the life of Plotinus just as one **visionary** <note>original: "illuminé," referring to someone claiming special divine inspiration or mystical insight.</note> might write the life of another. Unfortunately, nothing remains of Porphyry’s fifteen books against our Religion except for what is found in the works of **Ecclesiastical** <note>Church-related</note> Authors; and this is perhaps the greatest loss Christianity has ever suffered:

The fine name of **Theurgy** <term>theurgy: from the Greek *theourgia*, meaning "divine work," it refers to rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or achieve a state of union with the divine</term> did not deceive anyone (1); and even if we assume that the marvelous tales recorded in the history of that time regarding this subject are real, they could only be attributed to the Devil. <note>The author writes from a traditional Christian perspective, where any "supernatural" act performed outside of the Church was viewed as demonic rather than divine.</note> But the zeal of **Constantius** <note>Constantius II (reigned 337–361 AD), a son of Constantine the Great, who was known for his strict laws against pagan sacrifice and magic.</note> against superstitions suspected of magic did not allow the Philosophers to present themselves as Teachers initiated in the science of foreseeing the future through communication with the Gods. When a young man arrives and falls into the hands and power of those who have captured him (whether he came voluntarily or was forced), they subject him to this Attic custom, a game mixed with serious business. First, he is received as a guest by one of those who first seized him—whether they be friends, relatives, compatriots, or those who excel in the art of Sophistry and bring profit to their masters, and for that reason are held in the highest honor and value by them; for it serves as their reward to have those who look after their interests. 

Then he is harassed by everyone with mockery; this, if I am not mistaken, they do to humble the spirits of the newcomers and bring them under their power from the start. He is harassed more boldly by some and more eruditely by others, depending on whether he has rustic and inept manners or is endowed with urbanity. And this indeed seems very horrifying and inhuman to those who are unaware of it, but to those who have experienced it before, it is quite pleasant and sweet. For this is more a display of threats than the reality itself. 

Then he is led through the forum to the **bath** <note>The public baths were a central social hub; this "baptism" into student life was a common hazing ritual.</note> with a procession; the procession is conducted in this manner: those performing the duty of leading the youth are arranged in order, separated by equal spaces, and they precede him two by two to the bath. These customs indicate a great multitude of **Students**, and we could moreover conclude this from the emulation or the jealousy that existed between those from different countries. **Saint Gregory** (1) speaks of this himself regarding **Saint Basil**, and thus allows us to judge how numerous these schools must have been.

During the interval between the death of **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who introduced mystical and ritualistic elements (theurgy) into Platonism.</note> and the reign of **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD) was the last pagan emperor of Rome; he attempted to restore Hellenistic religion after the empire had turned toward Christianity.</note>—which lasted twenty-five to thirty years—the disciples of **Iamblichus**, who were numerous, being unable to teach in freedom, dispersed into various provinces, and thereby perhaps spread their sentiments even further. But as if they had been on the lookout, when **Julian** revealed his inclination toward the **Pagan Religion**, they were ready to give him lessons suited to his taste and to confirm him in his hatred of **Christianity**.

### Critical History

Among these Philosophers we count **Aedesius**, **Eusebius**, **Chrysanthius**, and especially **Maximus of Ephesus** <note>Maximus of Ephesus (c. 310–372 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and a key influence on Emperor Julian, known for his mastery of theurgy and magic.</note>. **Aedesius** was from Cappadocia. His father, more distinguished by his noble birth than by his wealth, had his son study to enable him to accumulate some. But **Aedesius** was eager only to enrich his mind with the treasures of the Sciences, and he succeeded with such success that he was little inferior to his Master **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus was the founder of the Syrian school of Neoplatonism; his teachings shifted the philosophy from pure logic toward ritual and mysticism.</note>. It is claimed that due to his great reputation, **Julian**, before becoming Emperor, wished to converse with him, and was astonished to find such strength of mind in such an elderly man. Had it depended on this Prince, he would not have parted from him until **Aedesius** had shared all his knowledge with him. **Aedesius** stood firm, and insisted on delegating the care of instructing **Julian** to his two Disciples, **Eusebius** and **Chrysanthius**.

But these two did not agree on the value that should be placed on <term>Theurgic operations</term> <note>Theurgy, from the Greek *theourgia* ("god-working"), involves rituals and ceremonies designed to invoke the presence of the gods or achieve a union with the divine, moving beyond mere intellectual philosophy.</note>. **Chrysanthius** held them in high regard; and **Eusebius** despised them, or feigned to despise them. Proclus was very industrious; he had acquired much knowledge, but it remained in his mind as a confused and poorly digested mass. It appears from those of his writings which still remain to us that he composed them with precipitation, without giving himself the time to correct them, piling up everything the Ancients had said as if their opinions had been the same. Justinian <note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD), the Byzantine Emperor known for his legal reforms and his efforts to enforce Christian orthodoxy.</note> could no longer tolerate a completely Pagan Philosophy being taught at Athens. He forbade it by his laws. The Platonic Philosophers saw this zeal as a persecution, from which they resolved to protect themselves by taking refuge in the territories of the King of Persia <note>Specifically, the court of Khosrow I, who was known as a patron of the arts and philosophy.</note>. They flattered themselves that they would be well received there. But their hopes were deceived; and they had no other recourse but to return (1) to the lands of the Empire. Thus, once peace had been established between Justinian and Chosroes, the Philosophers took the opportunity to return to the Provinces dependent on the Romans. This event dates from the year five hundred and thirty-three. And since then, one no longer hears mention in History of Platonic Philosophy. As for the Sectarians <note>In this 18th-century context, "Sectarians" refers to Protestants or members of other Christian denominations outside the Catholic Church.</note>, who from childhood have allowed themselves to be filled with prejudices against the Catholic Church, a thousand doubts ought to arise in their minds regarding the preference that, without full knowledge of the matter, they have given to their own Communion <note>A specific religious denomination or branch of the church.</note>. If they happen to waver in their belief, it is because they had not understood the strength of the motives one has for never separating from it.

If one excepts from this discourse a few historical traits for which there are no witnesses to cite, and assuming, moreover, that one does not believe in Christianity, then this discourse may seem reasonable enough. These were also the dispositions held by the early Christians toward the Pagans and the Philosophers.

# ->On Eclecticism.<-

I have, however, suggested that one cannot justify the facts that the Encyclopedist <note>A contributor to the *Encyclopédie*, the landmark Enlightenment project known for its often skeptical and secular viewpoint.</note> puts forward. Where, indeed, did he find that the progress and intolerance of Christianity brought about the birth of Eclecticism? Was Potamon <note>A philosopher from Alexandria, traditionally credited with founding the Eclectic sect around the 1st century.</note> thinking of Christianity when he invented his new method of philosophizing? One can only say so by mere guesswork. Later on, the Eclectic philosophers, or the New Platonists <note>Often called Neoplatonists today; they were a school of mystical philosophy that heavily influenced—and later rivaled—early Christian thought.</note>, became the greatest enemies of Christianity. But we are concerned here with the beginning of their sect. Now, the disputes of the other sects must naturally have produced Eclecticism. For the only advantage gained from the philosophical battles that had lasted for several centuries was to provide weapons to the Sceptics <note>A school of thought that argued human reason is incapable of reaching certain truth, often pointing to the endless disagreements between other philosophers as proof.</note>, the most unreasonable of all philosophers. Thus, everything invited one to follow Potamon’s method, which, by the Encyclopedist's own admission, ought to have been adopted sooner. Thus Diogenes Laërtius (1) <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> [tells] us

In the time of Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor, who attempted to suppress Christianity and revive traditional Greco-Roman religion.</note>, the fear of persecution, the desire to win the favors of the Court, the love of pleasures, and a hatred for a Christian life, were able to create apostates. But it is against all probability to attribute these apostasies to the excesses of the Eclectics offering human victims. It is likewise a more than risky conjecture to attribute the conversion of some Eclectics to these same excesses. These conversions have known causes, for which one should not substitute others invented at will. It was then the time of the Gospel Harvest <note>A metaphorical term for a period of significant growth and conversion within the early Church.</note>. Christianity shone with a radiance that could only increase the number of its partisans.

The Fates have not granted them the favors nor the knowledge of immortal Jupiter <note>The supreme deity of the Roman pantheon.</note>.

# Critical History

One must admit, it is a bizarre assortment of the most disparate ideas to believe, all at once, that Jesus Christ is a Person of excellent wisdom whose Soul was received into the dwelling of the Blessed; and yet to condemn his Religion: to persuade oneself that one can, after several centuries, be better informed of the Doctrine of Jesus Christ than the Apostles were: to suppose that God favored them with the gift of Miracles, and that they gave their lives for the Religion of their Master, after having altered it in the fundamental point of the Worship of God. It is nevertheless certain, by unimpeachable witnesses, that some among the Pagans held roughly these thoughts.

One cannot help but feel that Synesius was not taken for a man imbued with erroneous opinions when he was consecrated as Bishop.

Even if one were to agree, however, that Constantine had not composed this **Discourse** himself, one would not dare to dispute that he had adopted it, that he had made it his own, that he had recited it publicly, and that he had recited others like it; which is enough to establish that he was much more learned than princes usually are. He had particularly directed his reflections toward the proofs of **Christianity**. He had thought much on the vanity and the absurdity of **Idolatry**. Could he then believe that the **Philosophers**, with all their magic, could chain the winds? Would the **Bishops** by whom he was almost always surrounded have left him in this superstition, which was worse than childish? Constantine, although he was not yet baptized, had been a Christian for more than twenty years when he put **Sopater** <note>Sopater of Apamea was a Neoplatonist philosopher and former friend of Constantine. # Critical History

<margin>(1) "If Julian had reigned for a few years... the Christian name would have been finished throughout the extent of the Empire. leads one to judge that these projects are attributed to Julian with a fair degree of likelihood and foundation (1).

> "If Julian had reflected on what had happened to himself, he would have been convinced that instead of forbidding study to the Christians, he had nothing better to do than to open the Schools of Eclecticism <note>In this context, "Eclecticism" refers to the Neoplatonic philosophy of the later Roman Empire, which sought to harmonize various philosophical traditions into a single mystical system.</note> to them. They would have been infallibly attracted there by the extreme conformity of the principles of this Sect with the Dogmas of Christianity. The **Encyclopedist** <note>The author refers to the contributor of the "Eclecticism" entry in the *Encyclopédie*, the landmark secular dictionary of the Enlightenment edited by Diderot and d’Alembert.</note> could hardly have told us, in a more explicit way, that the proofs of **Christianity** do not seem to him to hold up under philosophical scrutiny. It is enough to read this text carefully to be convinced of it. But it is superfluous to insist further on a matter that is well enough known.

It would be foolishness not to understand that the **Encyclopedist** <note>Referring to the author of the article in the *Encyclopédie*, whose skeptical subtext the current author is trying to expose.</note>, through ironic language, insults those who believe in the **miracle** of which he speaks. Let us reason with him, then, as though we fully understand his language. He counts as nothing all the authorities who testify in favor of the **prodigy** <term>prodigy: an extraordinary event or marvel seen as a sign of divine intervention</term>, because this prodigy—according to what he claims—converted no one: neither **Julian**, whose plans it thwarted; nor **Ammianus Marcellinus**, who records it; nor the **Jews**, who were witnesses to it and who felt its fearsome effects. His reasoning, therefore, rests on this implied principle: that one should not place any faith in marvels that did not convert those who could not doubt their certainty. Thus, according to the **Encyclopedist**, one should not place faith in the **Resurrection of Lazarus**, in that of **Jesus Christ**, in the **multiplication of the loaves**, and in so many other **miracles** which failed to persuade the **Jews** that **Jesus Christ** was the **Messiah**.

The best-attested **miracles** do not constitute proofs against which stubbornness and prejudice cannot—and very often do—resist. **Ammianus Marcellinus** <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian; though a pagan, he famously recorded the "miraculous" fire that stopped Julian’s attempt to rebuild the Jewish Temple.</note> believed the **prodigy** that occurred in **Jerusalem**, without concluding that it was necessary to become a **Christian**, because he was persuaded, like many others (1), that it was not through a single form of **religious worship** that one could please the **Divinity**. A building whose foundations could not even be laid cannot be "overthrown." Julian was too fine a rhetorician for us to attribute such improper language to him. Thus, it seems to me that one can resolve this difficulty differently, even without adopting the idea that the Temple was destroyed by **Herod**. For one could hardly venture to say that what Herod did to embellish the Temple and make it more magnificent constituted its second overthrow. I would therefore believe that Julian, a very well-educated Prince, had in mind an event from the reign of **Hadrian** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 117–138 AD); after the Bar Kokhba revolt, he leveled what remained of Jerusalem to build a Roman colony.</note>. Julian <note>The text begins mid-word from the previous page, "lien," completing the name "Julien" or Julian.</note> wanted to rebuild the Temple. He says so, (1) and he says, in effect, that he was unable to do it. But was it men who placed an obstacle in the way of his plan? He was the master of the empire. It could only be Heaven <note>The author implies a divine or supernatural intervention, reflecting historical accounts of fire or earthquakes that stopped the construction in 363 AD.</note> that rendered his enterprise useless.

This admission by Julian is found in a work he composed shortly before his death. In it, acting in his capacity as Sovereign Pontiff <note>As Roman Emperor, Julian held the title *Pontifex Maximus*, the high priest of the state religion.</note>, he provides instructions to the priests of Paganism. He seeks to reform the disorders and abuses for which the ministers of idolatrous worship <note>The author uses "idolatrous worship" to describe ancient Roman religion, reflecting the perspective of the 18th-century historiography in which this book was likely written.</note> could be blamed, aiming to make them models of virtue. Julian reveals himself in these writings; his mind and character are discovered there unequivocally. Never was a piece of writing less suspect—or less deserving of suspicion—of being a forgery; indeed, no one is known to have doubted its authenticity.

The power of Demons being subordinate to that of God, no solid reason obliges us to believe that God often allows them to use it.

Demons are perhaps the authors of what appears to surpass human strength and industry. But one rarely has good evidence that they do so. They can make their presence felt by making frightful specters appear. But the difficulty lies in establishing these apparitions through trustworthy witnesses. It has finally been understood that the alleged <term>Sorcerers<gloss>In this context, individuals accused of witchcraft or entering into pacts with the devil.</gloss></term>, who accused themselves of having attended nocturnal assemblies of the <term>Sabbath<gloss>The "Sabbat" or Witches' Sabbath, a folkloric midnight meeting of those practicing witchcraft.</gloss></term>, should rather be dismissed as <term>visionaries<gloss>A term used by Enlightenment thinkers to describe people suffering from delusions or an overactive imagination rather than spiritual possession.</gloss></term> than punished as guilty. The same motives that might induce villains to enter into commerce with the Demon might induce them to feign that they actually maintain this commerce; and even if one could be certain of their sincerity, how could one be certain they are not the dupes of their imagination?

...make another reflection, regarding the supernatural occurrences of Paganism. Although these arguments have some appearance of truth, they are countered by opposite reasons and examples. If men love their opinions <note>Original: "sentimens." In this context, it refers to intellectual convictions or religious beliefs.</note>, they love their comfort, their peace, and their possessions even more; and when faced with the necessity of renouncing one or the other, the scales do not remain balanced for long.

A few men, possessing a singular character, wish to distinguish themselves by remaining constant in their convictions; but the majority, being weak, yield to the motivations arising from natural inclinations. We have seen even the true Religion <note>The author refers here to Catholicism.</note> die out in Africa under the rule of the Muslims, where it is tolerated. Christianity is nearly annihilated in other countries because it is oppressed there. No trace of it remains in Japan, where it once flourished <note>A reference to the brutal suppression of Christianity in Japan during the 17th century, following the Shimabara Rebellion.</note>. The ancient cults of European and Asian Paganism would no longer be known if their memory had not been preserved in books.

### Critical History

In all these examples, the sustained persecution born of ignorance has produced its natural effect: the destruction of the persecuted religions.

Nevertheless, the Jews preserve themselves under the harshest oppression. But this is, if I dare say so, the work of (1) Providence. Both this oppression and this survival were foretold. Christianity became more flourishing the more cruelly it was persecuted; but this too was the work of God. God had announced these persecutions; He had announced the conversion of the world, which was their fruit. In these cases, it is man who fights against God; it is therefore man who will succumb.

In other circumstances, the greatest forces prevail, and persecution triumphs, unless specific circumstances <note>Original: "conjonctures particulières."</note> make it weaker than the passions that resist it.

# On Eclecticism

...[Chris]tianity, which undergo neither revolutions nor metamorphoses, and which cannot become philosophical opinions subject to the examination of human reason. Yet it concerns a famous man, honored as a *Saint* by the Greek Church and by the Latin Church, who is accused of a horrible crime without there being any admissible witness or one not suspected of partiality. For *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439 AD), a contemporary church historian known for his relatively objective accounts, though often critical of the clergy.</note>, who is not favorable toward him in his account of this event, does not say that the Patriarch was informed of the plot formed against *Hypatia*. This historian relates only that the people, having conjectured from the frequent conversations between *Hypatia* and the Prefect *Orestes* that she was preventing him from reconciling with the Patriarch, were driven by anger. Led by *Peter* the Reader <note>A minor cleric in the Alexandrian church; his leadership of the mob is a central point of contention regarding the Church's official involvement.</note>, they formed the design of seizing *Hypatia*, and they crowned their crime in the manner just reported. *Socrates* does not say, nor does he insinuate (1), that *St. Cyril* had any part in it. Blame was nevertheless cast upon him because he was the occasion for it. But was not *Orestes*, in his obstinate refusal to reconcile with *St. Cyril*, even more the occasion—and an occasion that was not innocent before the tribunal of any impartial judge?

->## Concerning Eclecticism ##<-

The Encyclopedist <note>Likely a reference to the authors of the French *Encyclopédie*, such as Diderot or d'Alembert, who were often critical of Church history and the character of Saint Cyril.</note> asserts against St. Cyril the haughtiness and impetuosity of his character. But without debating whether this accusation is well-founded, is it to people of a haughty and fiery character that one commonly attributes the darkest conspiracies? Those capable of concealing a plan for vengeance under a mask of moderation are better suited for such things. No one has suggested that this was the character of St. Cyril.

But it is claimed he secured impunity for Peter the Reader, who incited the riot of which Hypatia <note>Hypatia (c. 350–415 AD), a famous Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer, and mathematician in Alexandria whose death at the hands of a mob became a focal point for critiques of early Christian intolerance.</note> was the victim. I respond that this is stated solely on the testimony of the Author, copied by Suidas <note>The *Suda* (or Suidas), a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia. The "Author" mentioned is likely Damascius, a pagan philosopher whose writings were often hostile to the Christian clergy.</note>, who should not be believed when testifying against St. Cyril. One may, however, conjecture that St. Cyril concerned himself with obtaining a pardon for those who had massacred Hypatia. At that time, Bishops used to solicit (1) the pardon of those who had been condemned.

## Critical History

Mr. Lacroze. But he should have remembered that the ancient Church was not in the habit of tempering its expressions when it wished to demonstrate its horror for the Heresiarchs <note>A "heresiarch" is the founder or leader of a heretical movement.</note> and for their errors. It intended to inspire similar sentiments in its children (1).

One cannot, without slandering it, accuse the Council of having acted with haste in the condemnation of Nestorius. This arrogant man was obstinate in his errors. The Acts of the Council <note>The "Acts" are the official recorded proceedings and documents of an ecclesiastical council.</note> contain evident proof of this, and everything that had occurred over the previous three years left no doubt on the matter. Since the Fathers of the Council were witnesses to Nestorius’s defiance <note>original: "contumace," referring to a stubborn refusal to obey authority.</note>, why should they have suspended the sentence? It was unanimous, and if they had awaited the arrival of the Easterners <note>The "Orientaux" or Easterners refers to the bishops from the region of Antioch, led by John of Antioch, who were delayed in arriving at Ephesus and were suspected of being sympathetic to Nestorius.</note>, the Council would have degenerated into a riot. There was even reason to fear that blood would be spilled. It was, therefore, the result of singular prudence—or rather, a visible stroke of Providence—to have seized the proper moment to expel the Heresiarch from the See of Constan- <note>The text breaks here; it refers to the See of Constantinople, the bishopric held by Nestorius before his deposition.</note>

However, it will be no less glorious for St. Cyril, even if one supposes that he was the sole author of the expulsion of the Jews. When viewing this event from this perspective, it will appear incredible, and one will certainly wish to soften it—that is to say, to change its most revolting circumstances; this amounts to abandoning the account of **John of Salisbury** <note>John of Salisbury (c. 1120–1180) was an influential English philosopher and bishop who, in his work *Policraticus*, recorded the claim that Pope Gregory I burned the Palatine Library to ensure the Scriptures were not overshadowed by secular literature.</note> and having no guarantee for the accusation made against the holy **Pontiff**.

This writer of the twelfth century reported it based on a supposed tradition; as if such an authority were sufficient to make one adopt a morally impossible <note>In this context, "morally impossible" refers to something that is so contrary to a person’s known character and the common behavior of humanity that it cannot be believed.</note> account. The tradition in question is purely oral, as no known author before him had recorded it in their writings. There are nearly six centuries between the death of **St. Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD).</note> and that of **John of Salisbury**.

### on Eclecticism.

...obstinacy, the **Eclectics** <note>The Eclectics were a school of philosophy that did not hold to a single set of dogmas but instead selected what they considered the best parts of various existing systems.</note> find themselves committed to becoming the enemies of **Christianity**, and the **Apologists** <note>An "Apologist" is someone who offers a formal defense or justification of a doctrine or belief—in this case, the traditional polytheistic religions of the ancient world.</note> of **Paganism**.

I say first "enemies of **Christianity**"; not because **Christian Worship** was so depraved that **God** rejected it; the **Eclectics** were careful not to think so—they who, by a fundamental principle of their morality, condemned no form of **Religion**. I say further that the **Eclectics** were forced to become the **Apologists** of the **Idolatrous Religion**. Was the greatest of the **Gods** <note>Referring to Zeus (Jupiter), whose myths included numerous acts of violence and infidelity.</note> not the most notorious villain? His father, his brothers, and his children were no better than he. They possessed the vices of men, yet lacked their virtues.

But I ask: if the **Poets** who invented them—or, if one prefers, who were simply the **Historians** of the fables attributed to the **Pagan Divinities**—foresaw that they were putting the ignorant common people at risk of introducing into their **Worship** all the infamies told of these **Divinities**? If, despite this premonition, the **Poets** did not hesitate to hide truths as trivial as they were useless under the veil of **allegories**, whose literal meaning draped these **Divinities** in the most shameful weaknesses; and if, moreover, to better instill these fables into the people’s memory, the **Poets** dressed them in all the charms of harmonious verse, do they deserve to be seen as anything other than public poisoners?

### ARTICLE II.

*The Axiom, **nothing comes from nothing**, <note>original: "rien ne se fait de rien"; a reference to the classical principle "ex nihilo nihil fit."</note> provided the Epicureans <note>Followers of the philosopher Epicurus, who argued that the universe was composed of eternal atoms and that no divine creator was necessary.</note> with victorious weapons against all the ancient Philosophers. The absurdities into which one falls when denying the possibility of Creation. Could God know matter if He were not its Creator? When the possibility of Creation is denied, one can assign the causes of neither the movement and qualities of matter, nor of our sensations. The Creator can give intelligent beings the faculty to modify themselves. The inconsistency of those Philosophers who have recognized or do recognize this faculty in themselves, and yet continue to deny the possibility of Creation.*

Let us examine errors of another kind, and of a more philosophical nature, if

I may speak thus. All the ancient philosophers fell into it; and despite the light that Christianity had already spread, the Neoplatonists <note>A school of mystical philosophy that arose in the 3rd century AD, attempting to reconcile Plato’s ideas with other spiritual traditions.</note> did not know how, or did not wish, to guard themselves against it. These wanderings all had a common origin. It was this philosophical prejudice adopted by the Eclectics <note>Philosophers who did not adhere to a single system but "selected" (from the Greek *eklektikos*) what they believed were the best doctrines from various schools.</note> as by all other sects: nothing exists that has not always existed in terms of its substance, or *nothing comes from nothing* <note>original: "rien ne se fait de rien"; the classical principle *ex nihilo nihil fit*, which suggests matter is eternal and cannot be created by a divine being.</note>: a too-fruitful error, which has had the most terrible influences on Theology and Philosophy. The greatest minds of antiquity, having adopted this alleged axiom, also adopted almost inconceivable errors. They first unanimously concluded that the matter of which this world is composed is eternal and unproduced. But some of them were careful not to stop at this first consequence; and here is how they reasoned. If the matter that composes bodies owes its existence only to itself, why should it not also owe its disposition and arrangement to itself? The necessity that makes a being exist also makes it exist in a certain state; and since

Thus, the hypotheses of Plato <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC) argued in the *Timaeus* that a "Demiurge" or divine craftsman organized pre-existing chaotic matter into the cosmos.</note> and Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "Mind" (*Nous*) acted upon a primordial mass to initiate motion and order.</note> contradict the great principle *that nothing is made from nothing.* <note>original: "que rien ne se fait de rien"; a translation of the Latin axiom *ex nihilo nihil fit*.</note> He who cannot give existence to matter can give it neither movement nor qualities.

And let it not be said that, without being able to give movement to matter, one can still regulate this movement when it is nothing but disorder and confusion. For when one cannot produce movement, how could one direct it? Is a movement produced but not directed not a contradiction in terms?

If it is a contradiction for a portion of matter to begin to exist, the same contradiction would hold regarding every other portion of matter, whether existing or possible. It would be a contradiction for matter not to be infinite; for there to be any space empty of matter; or for matter not to be eternal, whether in the past <note>original: "*a parte ante*"; a Scholastic term referring to eternity stretching backward into the past.</note> or toward the future <note>original: "*a parte post*"; referring to eternity stretching forward into the future.</note>; finally, it would be a contradiction for this matter to be divisible: for that which is infinite can be neither increased nor diminished. Now, that which is divisible has parts that compose it; and parts have finite boundaries. Thus, the infinite would be composed of finite parts: a pure contradiction.

Let us reflect on the consequences of this alleged impossibility of Creation. If God does not have the power to give existence to even the smallest portion of matter, then one attributes to Him the power to set the matter of the Universe in motion without any logical basis, and there is no longer any reason not to throw oneself into the abyss of atheism. Is one very far from [atheism], when one asserts only by chance that God can set in motion all the matter of the Universe? He who is uncertain on that point must be uncertain whether there is a God. These consequences are only too closely linked. If God cannot produce the smallest part of matter, it is doubtful whether He can move all the matter of the Universe; if it is doubtful whether He can move any part of it, it is doubtful whether there is a God. One <term>gratuitously</term><note>In philosophical arguments, to grant something "gratuitously" means to assume it is true without providing any proof or logical necessity.</note> gives God the attribute of supreme mover if one refuses Him the attribute of Creator. There is no difference between limiting God's power and denying it; nor between denying His power and denying His existence.

The qualities of matter present another difficulty, to which the enemies of creation <note>The author refers to philosophers who argue that matter is eternal and was not created from nothing by a divine being.</note> had nothing reasonable to say in response. Let us explain. Reason rebels against a system that attributes all the beauties of the Universe to chance. But does it rebel any less against a system that attributes to a blind necessity the qualities which make the parts of matter fit for the construction of the Universe, & of the bodies that compose it? The first of these two systems belongs to Epicurus, & the second to Anaxagoras.

Mr. le Batteux (1) presented this latter system in its best light; but he was careful not to undertake to justify it based on the **similar parts** <term>similar parts: Referring to "homeomeries," a theory by Anaxagoras suggesting that matter is composed of minute particles that have the same nature as the whole (for example, gold is made of tiny gold particles).</term>: qualities that the Epicureans did not attribute to their atoms. Anaxagoras was right to call upon an *intelligence* <note>In Greek philosophy, Anaxagoras's "Nous" or Mind/Intelligence is the force that set the primordial matter in motion to create the universe.</note> for the formation of the Universe, since one cannot suppose that it is the work of chance. To have the world emanate from the **Supreme Being** <note>The "Supreme Being" refers to God, but in this philosophical context, it often refers to the "First Principle" or the "One."</note> is to annihilate the dogma of creation: it is to degrade the **Supreme Being**: it is to turn him into a monstrous assemblage of all the Beings of the Universe.

Thus, several **New Platonists** <note>Also known as Neo-Platonists, a school of mystical philosophy that arose in the 3rd century AD, seeking to synthesize the works of Plato with other traditions.</note> had adopted another method to harmonize **Plato** and **Aristotle**; and without renouncing their view on the impossibility of creation, they attempted to draw closer to **Christian Theology**. This was to say that God had produced the world from all eternity. By this, they granted to **Aristotle** that the world was eternal; they granted to **Plato** that God had formed the world—that the world was his work, but an eternal work. Finally, it might have seemed of little importance to Christians to hear it said that God had produced the world before all time, and consequently from all eternity; since in reality, there had been no time before the production of the world. But one should have perceived the trap hidden in this language of the **New Platonists** <note>Also known as Neo-Platonists, these philosophers attempted to synthesize Greek thought with mystical elements, often arguing that the world flows out of God like light from a sun.</note>. Is a world produced from all eternity a world that God created, to which he gave existence? An **eternal Creation** is a contradiction in terms. The word **Creation** signifies, on the part of the creature, an existence that it has received; an existence that has begun, and which did not exist before. On the part of the **Creator**, **Creation** signifies an existence which he has given and which he had not given before. The term **eternal** excludes all these ideas. An eternal world has always existed; and it implies that it was produced; or if it was really produced, it is not truly eternal.

It seems that God, being omnipotent, should also be able to exercise his omnipotence from all eternity. But it is repugnant to the nature of a created thing to be eternal. In what sense then could the **Neo-Platonists** <note>The author uses the term "New Platonists" to refer to the school of thought beginning with Plotinus in the 3rd century AD, which sought to harmonize Plato's philosophy with mystical and religious concepts.</note> claim that God had produced the world from all eternity? They could do so in a metaphysical sense and through (1) abstraction. God could not have really and physically produced what had always existed; and the Neo-Platonists could not assert this without error. But they could conceive of a priority of order in the cause which, according to them, brought the world into existence. In their **Metaphysics**, God was not really before the world: he had not produced it; but they conceived that he existed before, that he was anterior by a priority of cause; an ideal and not a real priority. Now, an ideal priority is not sufficient for a real **Creation**. ### Critical History

Imagine, says Mr. Mosheim, (1) that Jupiter has held a golden chain in his hand for all eternity: and imagine at the same time that three Philosophers are disputing among themselves whether the gold from which this chain is composed—insofar as one can mentally separate it from the chain—exists from all eternity, or whether it comes from the hand of Jupiter, or whether it was created from nothing. What would one judge of this frivolous dispute? By the very hypothesis, this chain is eternal; the gold composing it has therefore never begun to exist. Thus, what use would there be in asking what this gold would be, had it existed or been created before forming the chain? This is a faithful image of the disputes of the **New Platonists** <note>The author refers to the Neo-Platonists, like Plotinus and Porphyry, who argued that the world emanates eternally from God.</note>. Does the matter of a world supposed to be eternal come from God, is it uncreated, has it existed eternally? These questions are as senseless as asking: *Did the matter of an eternal world exist before being the matter of that world?*

If it seemed possible to them that a substance should exist from all eternity because God wills it, why did they not find it possible that God could make it exist in time by the same effect of His will? One could not give a good reason why God could not create the world in time, if He could produce it from all eternity.

### On Eclecticism

...[never even a] true union between the **common soul** <note>original: "ame commune," often referred to in philosophy as the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul</note> and the **individual souls**, which are claimed to be portions of it, as soon as one supposes that the common soul is **material**. Portions of a **material Being** are themselves material Beings. Now, material Beings that can be counted and separated from one another each constitute a "whole." One can only regard them as parts of a whole through a **fiction of the mind** <note>that is, a mental construct rather than a physical reality</note>, which considers as a single whole that which actually comprises several wholes. Thus, in the supposition that the common soul is material, the individual souls—which are claimed to be portions of it that must one day reunite with it to have only a common existence—neither were nor will ever become portions of it, except in the most improper sense; much like small piles of sand heaped upon one another together make a single pile.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But what a collection of absurdities if our **Philosophers** were to say that the common soul was **immaterial** and **indivisible**! # Critical History

material and indivisible. There is a contradiction in wanting an **immaterial Being** to actually emanate from another **immaterial Being**. Indivisibility excludes emanation <note>In philosophy, "emanation" is the idea that everything flows out from a single source, like light from a sun; the author argues that if the source is truly one and indivisible, it cannot "give off" parts of itself.</note>. Thus, those who—in order to avoid the **Dogma of the creation of spirits**—have them emanate from the **Divinity**, or from a **common soul** <note>original: "ame commune," referring to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul</note> which itself emanates from the Divinity, utter nothing but unintelligible discourse if one examines their meaning; otherwise, they turn the **Divine substance** into a material substance. To say, in effect, that Spirits come from God, and that they owe Him their origin, means either that God brought them into existence by an act of His good pleasure—in other words, that He **created** them—or it means that He communicated a portion of His substance to them: a manifest contradiction if God is an indivisible substance. The same reflection applies if one speaks of **material Beings**: to say that they emanate from God, that they have come out of His bosom, is either to say nothing of which one can form any idea, or it is to say that they existed within the substance of God before their emanation.

# Critical History

In the disputes between the Pagans and the Christians, the <term>Jewish Religion<gloss>Refered to here as "Religion Judaïque." In this period, scholars emphasized that Christianity was rooted in the much older legal and prophetic tradition of the Hebrews.</gloss></term> made common cause with Christianity. The latter could not be a divine Religion unless that of <term>Moses<gloss>The biblical prophet and lawgiver; early Christians used his historical antiquity to claim that their roots were older and more "authentic" than those of Greek philosophy.</gloss></term> were also divine. Our <term>Apologists<gloss>Early Christian writers (like Justin Martyr or Origen) who wrote formal defenses of their faith to explain it to the Roman authorities and Pagan intellectuals.</gloss></term> were therefore obliged to defend the Jewish Religion against the Pagans, to highlight its wisdom, its holiness, and its antiquity. They had to insist strongly on the fact that Moses, being much earlier than all the Legislators and all the Sages of Greece, could not have taken anything from them; instead, those Legislators and Sages might have profited from what was contained in the <term>Books of Moses<gloss>The Pentateuch, or the first five books of the Bible.</gloss></term>. This is also what the <term>Fathers<gloss>The "Church Fathers," influential bishops and theologians of the first few centuries of the Christian Church.</gloss></term> executed in the most triumphant manner.

They could have—let us add, if you will, that they should have—stopped there. Their victory was complete. But they wanted to push it further. They claimed that, in effect, <term>Plato<gloss>The famous Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) whose ideas about the soul and the divine often seemed to mirror biblical concepts.</gloss></term> was the plagiarist of Moses: a hypothesis that is more than uncertain, as we shall soon discuss. It would have therefore been prudent not to engage in this discussion. For in <term>Polemical Books<gloss>Works written specifically to argue against or attack an opposing point of view.</gloss></term>, should one use arguments that cannot withstand the test of a severe exami- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("examen"), likely continuing on the next page to warn that using weak historical arguments can undermine a larger, valid defense.</note>

<summary>This page explains how early Christian Apologists defended their faith by linking it to the antiquity of Moses, while also critiquing their riskier claim that Plato "plagiarized" Hebrew scripture.</summary>

# On Eclecticism

[argu]ments? They lead away from the goal, which one must not lose sight of: the conviction of the Reader. One halts them, fatigues them, and if they possess intelligence, they are not persuaded. Truth suffers for it. A weak argument makes one suspect that the other proofs are no better. Finally, one does not place any trust in an Author who allows themselves to be dazzled by mere probabilities.

What crime, however, did the <term>Fathers of the Church<gloss>The influential Christian theologians and bishops of the first few centuries AD.</gloss></term> commit by adopting a sentiment that it does not appear the enemies of Christianity ever fought against? It seems rather that Jewish or Pagan writers followed this sentiment. 5th. The <term>Fathers<gloss>The influential theologians and writers of the early Christian Church whose works established the foundations of Christian doctrine.</gloss></term>, in disputing against the <term>Heretics<gloss>Individuals or groups whose beliefs were considered to be in contradiction with the established doctrines of the Church.</gloss></term>, employed <term>Platonic<gloss>Relating to the philosophy of Plato (c. 427–347 BC), which emphasizes the existence of abstract forms and the immortality of the soul; early Christians often used this framework to explain spiritual concepts.</gloss></term> expressions and hypotheses; and thereby they (1) altered the purity and integrity of some of the <term>dogmas<gloss>The core, authoritative principles or tenets of the Christian faith.</gloss></term> of the faith. We do not doubt that if it had been indicated, in a precise manner, what these alterations were, *Father Baltus* <note>Jean-François Baltus (1667–1743) was a French Jesuit theologian who wrote extensively to defend the early Church Fathers against the charge that they had "paganized" Christianity with Greek philosophy.</note> would have loudly vindicated them; and there is no <term>orthodox<gloss>Conforming to the traditionally accepted and established beliefs of the Church.</gloss></term> theologian who would not undertake it with confidence. The materials for the work that would need to be undertaken, to fulfill this purpose, would cost nothing to gather, and one would only need to put them to use. Let us pass to the sixth and final point. It is the most important of all, and the one where *Mr. Brucker* <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770) was a German historian of philosophy whose work, while scholarly, was often critical of the way early Christian writers merged faith with ancient Greek philosophy.</note> expresses himself with the least restraint. For one could imagine, either that this dogma being in effect within Plato's works, the Christians discovered it there and adopted it as an article of their belief; or that it was attributed to Plato without him having truly taught it, and that based on this false assumption, one nonetheless proceeded to make it a dogma of Christianity; or finally, that the <term>New Platonists<gloss>Also known as Neoplatonists, a school of mystical philosophy that arose in the 3rd century AD.</gloss></term>, since the establishment of the School of <term>Ammonius<gloss>Ammonius Saccas, a teacher in Alexandria considered one of the founders of Neoplatonism.</gloss></term> and <term>Plotinus<gloss>A major philosopher of the ancient world who systematized Neoplatonism.</gloss></term>, had imperceptibly slipped this dogma into the belief of the Christians.

But none of these hypotheses has the slightest probability; or rather, the contrary of what they state is certain. Thus, the effects of the alleged Platonism of the early Christians are nothing but imaginings without reality.

### ARTICLE III.

*The first Christians were raised in a spirit of aversion toward Pagan Philosophy, and the earliest Church Fathers condemned it. One could not have abandoned the doctrine of the Apostles to follow that of the Alexandrian School.* <note>The "Alexandrian School" refers to a tradition in Egypt where Christian scholars began to synthesize the Bible with Greek philosophy, a move the author of this text views with suspicion.</note>

It was not, however, impossible that these few truths might become contagious by sparking a hope of finding the full truth among them; and there can be no doubt that the writers of the New Testament intended to warn the early Christians against this temptation. This is clearly the aim of Saint Paul’s teachings. He could not have expressed himself more forcefully to inspire them with an aversion for Philo-

### Critical History

...each of them in particular, to persevere in the pure doctrine of the Apostles.

If, since the birth of Christianity, whether by way of reform or by way of explanation, any attempt was made to introduce some change in the faith of the Church, complaints were immediately made; the cry of "innovation" was raised; and recourse was had to anathemas <note>An anathema is a formal curse or excommunication by a religious authority, used to cast a person or an idea out of the community of faith.</note>. It is unheard of for even the slightest change to have been greeted in any other way. How, then, could Platonism, regarding the Trinity, have had a different fate? 

Did the Christian Doctors <term>Doctors of the Church: Renowned theologians whose teachings were influential in shaping official Christian doctrine.</term> divide their zeal between Plato and the Sacred Books, only to give the better portion to Plato, with the intent of making his sentiments prevail over those which the Church believed it had learned through Apostolic teaching? Were there then schools of Platonism to which Christian children were sent to draw the principles of Platonic philosophy? Had the vast majority of Pastors been raised in these schools? Did the majority make the reading of Plato's works their primary intellectual pursuit? Did the majority take pride in reconciling Plato with Scripture, and in finding the dogmas of the Gospel within the writings of Plato?

This servile spirit could not guide the **Fathers of the Church** when they read the **Pagan Philosophers**. They had shaken off that yoke simply by the fact that they had embraced **Christianity**. No longer regarding the **Philosophers** as their masters, the **Fathers** only subscribed to some of their opinions because they appeared to be founded on sound proofs. One must even observe that, before the **Eclectics** <note>Philosophers who select what they believe to be the best parts of various systems.</note> formed a specific **Philosophical School**, **Saint Clement of Alexandria** had said that he recognized as true **Philosophy** (1) only that which chose the truths spread throughout all the **Sects**, or in other words: **Eclectic Philosophy**. The method (2) of **Origen** <note>A prolific early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note>, when instructing his students, was in no way different from the **Eclectic** method. **Lactantius** <note>A counselor to Constantine the Great, known for his eloquent defense of Christianity.</note> approved (3) of no single **Sect**; but he claimed,

It would be too unreasonable to hold it against them as a crime.

One can only judge the sentiments of ancient authors by what they have written. If they spoke like the **Arians**, the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius (c. 256–336), who believed that Jesus was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to God the Father.</note> were not to be condemned for counting these authors as being on their side. In this Preface, which spans more than seventy pages, the Author firmly establishes the orthodoxy of the Fathers who lived prior to the *Council of Nicaea*; and no one has demonstrated that his proofs are not solid by claiming that he wrote them out of political necessity and against his true convictions. This Preface is little more than a tapestry of texts which speak very clearly in favor of Catholic dogma.

<header>on Eclecticism.</header>

**Saint Clement of Alexandria** <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150–215 AD), a theologian who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria and sought to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian faith.</note> was so enamored with the doctrine of **Plato** that he allowed it to infect his theology regarding the **Trinity**. <note>The central Christian doctrine that God is one essence in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> But can one, with any appearance of truth, say the same of **Saint Irenaeus** <note>Bishop of Lugdunum (modern Lyon) and a prominent early Christian apologist (c. 130–202 AD).</note> and **Tertullian**? <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage often called the "father of Latin theology."</note> Could Saint Irenaeus not have been biased against the sentiments of the Platonists, since he regarded them as the poisoned source (1) of the heresies he combated? (1) The Summary of the fourteenth chapter of the second Book of **Saint Irenaeus**'s *Against Heresies* <note>original: *Adversus Haereses*; Irenaeus’s most famous work, written to refute Gnosticism.</note> states that **Valentinus** <note>A mid-2nd century Gnostic teacher who founded the Valentinians.</note> and his followers had taken the principles of their doctrine from Pagan writers, changing nothing but the names. Another observation, no less important: the expressions favorable to the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who argued that the Son was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father.</note> that are found in the ecclesiastical authors who lived before the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The 325 AD council that defined the orthodox Christian belief in the Trinity against Arianism.</note> did not escape the notice of the Fathers who lived after this Council. (1) "How is it," you ask, "that there are several faulty things in their books? If I answer that I do not know the causes of these faults, I will not immediately judge them to be **heretics**. Or, certainly, before **Arius**—that noonday demon—was born in Alexandria, they spoke some things innocently and with less caution, which could not escape the slander of perverse men." <note>original: "Quomodo, inquies, in libris eorum vitioſa nonnulla ſunt? # On Eclecticism

...the divine substance, inseparable and indivisible, common to the Father and the Son; this is what Saint Justin believes, what he proves to the Jews, and what he announces to the Pagans. For it has been seen that what he teaches in his *Dialogue* <note>Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho*, a debate with a Jewish interlocutor.</note>, he also professes to believe in his great *Apology* addressed to the Emperors <note>Justin’s *First Apology*, addressed to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius to defend Christians against persecution.</note>.

However, despite such formal <note>In this context, "formal" means explicit and definitive.</note> texts concerning the consubstantiality <term>Consubstantiality: from the Latin *consubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance." It is the core orthodox belief that the Son is of the same divine essence as the Father.</term> of the Word, Saint Justin nevertheless says that the Son is the **Angel of the Father**, the **Minister of His will**: language that so shocked Father Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian and scholar who famously scrutinized the writings of the early Church Fathers for signs of Arianism.</note> that Saint Justin appeared to him to hold almost no other sentiment than that of the Arians <term>Arians: followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being and subordinate to the Father, rather than equal and eternal.</term>; as if those writers, whose orthodoxy is the least suspect, had not spoken in the very same way. The name *Angel*, given to the Son according to his Divine nature, carries no other significance than that of *Minister of the Father*. The Ancients were never accused of a crime for calling the Son, or the Word <note>original: "le Verbe," referring to the *Logos* or the pre-existent Christ.</note> not yet incarnate, the **Angel of the Father**. Both before and after the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of 325 AD which settled the divinity of Christ against Arian teachings.</note>, it was maintained that He who appeared to the Patriarchs, who is called God, and who is designated by the attributes most proper to the supreme God, is also called the **Angel of God**.
