Let us conclude with a reflection that is too natural to have not been frequently repeated, yet too decisive to be omitted. The <term>Church Fathers</term> <note>The influential theologians and writers in the early Christian Church who established the intellectual and doctrinal foundations of Christianity.</note> speak of the Son of God in an infinite number of places: sometimes of his divinity, sometimes of his humanity; sometimes of his equality with his Father, sometimes of his dependence; sometimes of his eternity and his <term>consubstantiality</term> <note>From the Latin *consubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance." They speak sometimes of his omnipotence and his other divine attributes, and sometimes of his qualities as Minister, Angel, and Counselor of God. The Theology of the Fathers would be truncated and incomplete, and they would have been unfaithful guardians of the <term>deposit of faith</term> <note>The body of revealed truth in the Scriptures and sacred tradition proposed by the Church for the belief of the faithful.</note>, if the collection of their texts did not state all of this regarding Jesus Christ. But what an injustice it is to accuse them of <term>heterodoxy</term> <note>Beliefs or doctrines that differ from the officially accepted "orthodox" positions of the Church.</note> simply because they did not write everything they believed about the Son of God in every single instance!

When, therefore, he ascends into your heart, he immediately speaks with you of justice, of modesty, of chastity, of kindness, of forgiveness, of charity, of piety. When all these things have ascended into your heart, know that the **Spirit of righteousness** is with you. Trust him, then, and his works. Receive now also the works of the **Spirit of iniquity**. First, he is bitter, angry, and foolish, and his works are ruinous, and they overthrow the servants of **God**. When, therefore, these things have ascended into your heart, you will understand from his works that this is the **Spirit of iniquity**. How, Lord, shall I understand? Listen, he says, and understand. When anger comes upon you, or bitterness, understand that he is in you: then the desire for many works, and the finest foods.... These things, then, when they have ascended into your heart, understand that the **Spirit of iniquity** is with you. *Hermas, book 2, mandate 6, vol. ### Critical History

The <term>false Saint Dionysius</term> <note>Referring to the author now known as Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an anonymous 5th-century theologian whose works were mistakenly attributed to a 1st-century convert of St. Paul.</note> puts forward the sentiments, or rather the daydreams, of the Alexandrian Philosophers of the fifth century, which are found in Proclus, who lived at that time. Every page of the false Saint Dionysius provides evidence of this. We know, moreover—I continue to relay the ideas of Mr. Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a German historian of philosophy who was highly critical of the Neoplatonic influence on Christianity.</note>—we know that the Works of the false Saint Dionysius, brought to France in the time of <term>Louis the Pious</term> <note>r. 814–840; the original French "le Débonnaire" refers to his easy-going or pious nature.</note>, were received there as a gift from Heaven.

His son, <term>Charles the Bald</term> <note>r. 840–877; a king of West Francia who was a notable patron of letters and the sciences.</note>, who loved the Sciences, had them translated into Latin by <term>John Scotus Eriugena</term> <note>An Irish theologian and philosopher who became a prominent intellectual at the Carolingian court.</note>. No one then doubted the authenticity of these Works; and they were not doubted until these last centuries, when the insights of a healthy criticism undeceived the Scholars, and almost universally convinced them that a forger had composed them under the name of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite.

Under this respectable name, they were regarded as a treasure of the most sublime Theology. They were read with eagerness, without suspecting that they contained pure <term>Pantheism</term> <note>The belief that the divine is identical with the universe, or that all things compose an all-encompassing, immanent God.</note>, or the system of <term>Emanations</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the idea that all reality flows or "emanates" from a central divine source, losing perfection as it descends.</note> of the Alexandrian Philosophers. Scotus Eriugena, who had translated them, was the devoted partisan—

Where does evil come from then? Evil, responds **St. Dionysius**, evil is nothing: evil is but a nothingness. It is a privation of being, a lack of being, for which the cause must be sought only in the creature, and in the imperfection that is inseparable from it. Despite its disorder, there is nevertheless in the creature some good and some being, of which God is the Author. This Theology, on which **St. Dionysius** never ceases to dwell, could not more formally exclude the principle of the non-production <note>The "non-production" (French: *improduction*) of matter refers to the philosophical belief that matter was never "made" or "produced" by a creator, but has existed eternally—a core tenet of many ancient systems that the author argues Dionysius rejects.</note> of matter. Now, the non-production of matter is the foundation of the **system of Emanations**.

# On Eclecticism

...in the mind? And if it were another idea, it would no longer be an act of love for God. What delusions! <note>Original: "chimeres." For if I have been able to banish the idea of him from my mind, then what I know at that moment, what I am attached to, is no longer the object of which I had an idea; it is no longer my God.

Thus, taking it *strictly* and *literally*, it is unintelligible language to say that one rids oneself of all the ideas one has of God; that one strips oneself of everything one has believed and been able to conceive of him, in order to know him better and to unite oneself more closely to him. # History *of Criticism*

Scripture speaks to us very often of the union of God with the inhabitants of Heaven, and yet tells us nothing of it that is entirely within our reach. In all the Holy Scriptures, there is no text that should give us clearer and more distinct notions of the state in which the Saints exist in Heaven than the passage where St. John says that we shall be like God, because we shall see him as he is (1). Nevertheless, despite this passage and many others, how many obscurities remain regarding the eternal happiness of the Saints?

What, then, can be known of the state in which God sometimes—and extraordinarily—places his servants in this present life, when he wishes to let them taste or glimpse something of what he reserves for them in the next life? It is a rash presumption to claim to snatch God's secret from him. <term>St. Paul<note>The Apostle Paul, whose account of being "caught up to the third heaven" in his second letter to the Corinthians is a foundational text for Christian mysticism.</note></term> did not know whether his <term>rapture<note>From the Latin *raptus*, referring to a state of being "carried away" or "caught up" in a divine vision or ecstasy, where the soul is temporarily detached from normal sensory experience.</note></term> into Heaven had occurred in his body or without his body (2). This ignorance should serve as a lesson to the <term>Mystics<note>Those who seek or describe direct, transformative experiences of the presence of God; here, the author refers specifically to writers who attempt to provide technical or rational explanations for these experiences.</note></term>. If they have solid reasons for it; let them...

# On Eclecticism.

Let them believe, if they wish, that God has granted them some favor which is not of the ordinary course of things. But let them not forget that sensible people are not obliged to believe them on their simple word. Even when one does not suspect their sincerity, one must suspect their imagination. For imagination alone produces the most vivid persuasion. God is the master of his gifts; he grants them to whomever he pleases. It is therefore possible that this or that person has been made a participant in the most intimate union with God. One cannot dispute the possibility of this favor. But regarding its reality, doubt is more than legitimate. The righteous man, the <term>visionary<note>In this context, a person who experiences visions or revelations that may be perceived by others as products of a disordered mind or overactive imagination rather than divine intervention.</note></term>, and the fraud can all equally assert that they have enjoyed the closest union with God. But his conscience accuses the fraud of his imposture. The other two may equally be acting in good faith, without the righteous man having any infallible means to convince himself, nor to convince others, that he is not under an illusion regarding this celestial favor. The gift of <term>discernment of spirits<note>A theological concept, notably discussed by St. Paul and later mystical writers, referring to the supernatural ability to judge whether a spiritual manifestation or impulse is truly divine, or whether it stems from human psychology or evil influences.</note></term> is a supernatural gift. One can claim it for oneself and not possess it in reality. How many <term>Fanatics<note>A term often used by Enlightenment-era writers to describe members of radical religious sects who claimed direct, private revelation to justify their actions or beliefs, often in opposition to reason or established church authority.</note></term> have claimed...

Miraculous favors in the order of <term>Grace<note>In Christian theology, Grace is the spontaneous and unmerited favor of God, often seen as a necessary gift for spiritual enlightenment or salvation that cannot be achieved by human effort alone.</note></term> depend only on the good pleasure of God; and if God has not revealed this to us in revelation, one cannot know either when or how He grants them. What has just been read in prose, Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619) was an Italian philosopher and free-thinker. Despite his use of theological language, he was convicted of atheism and pantheism, resulting in his tongue being cut out before he was burned at the stake in Toulouse.</note> repeated in verse at the end of his work. And although he had it printed in Lyon four years before his execution, I am not aware that it was ever treated as a crime. One could not, by the admission (1) of Mr. Abadie <note>Jacques Abadie (1654–1727) was a celebrated Protestant theologian whose works on the truth of the Christian religion were highly influential in the late 17th century.</note> himself, find these words condemnable except by the explanation one might give them; which signifies that one can give them a favorable interpretation. Indeed! Why should one refuse them the fairness granted to many similar texts (2) collected by Father Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), or Dionysius Petavius, was a French Jesuit theologian and scholar, famous for his work on the history of dogma.</note> in his *Theological Dogmas*; even though one could easily interpret them in a manner conforming to the system of Emanations <note>The "System of Emanations" is the belief that all things flow out of the divine essence. While common in Neoplatonism, it was often criticized by orthodox theologians who preferred the doctrine of creation *ex nihilo* (out of nothing).</note>.

This indulgence is all the more due to the Mystics, as they expressly warn that they do not wish their hyperbolic terms to be taken literally. These terms, in effect, seem to carry their own apology within them. The Mystics only employ them for lack of others sufficiently force[ful]—

to render what they conceive in the heat of their contemplations. Even these expressions seem too weak for their liking. From this arises, almost inevitably, a language of exaggeration, which must be brought back to a tempered interpretation. But instead of following the rules of this criticism, one attempts to discover some resemblance, on one side, between the ancient System of Emanations <term>System of Emanations: A philosophical theory, often linked to Neoplatonism, suggesting that all things flow out of the divine essence like light from a sun, rather than being created from nothing.</term> of the Oriental Philosophers, and the language of the Pseudo-St. Dionysius <note>The author refers to "S. Denys," known today as Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian whose works merged Christian thought with Neoplatonic philosophy. His writings were highly influential on later medieval mysticism.</note>, and the Mystics on the other. 

The discovery of this supposed genealogy of errors flatters a scholar. He spares no effort to give it the appearance of truth. It is, without doubt, what helped to seduce Mr. Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770) was a pioneering German historian of philosophy. His *Historia Critica Philosophiae* was famous for its rigorous, though often skeptical, analysis of historical systems of thought.</note>. For in the end, without proof—or rather, against the most evident proof—he accuses St. Dionysius of being a partisan of an impious system; he accuses the Church of having allowed the simplicity of the faith to be corrupted. Could one fail to alert the Public to such a proceeding? Could one fail to avenge the Church against such a glaring injustice?
